paper.title: 3rd International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics — Theoretical Competition

documentNotes.title: Please read these instructions carefully
documentNotes.statement:
1. Each student will receive problem sheets in English and/or in his/her native language.
2. The available time for answering theoretical problems is 5 hours. You will have 15 short problems (Theoretical Part 1, Problem 1 to 15), and 2 long problems (Theoretical Part 2, Problem 16 and 17).
3. Use only the pen that has been provided on your desk.
4. Do Not use the back side of your writing sheets. Write only inside the boxed area.
5. Yellow scratch papers are not considered in marking.
6. Begin answering each problem in separate sheet.
7. Fill in the boxes at the top of each sheet of your paper with your "country name", your "student code", "problem number", and total number of pages which is used to answer to that problem.
8. Write the final answer for each problem in the box, labeled "Answer Sheet".
9. Starting and the end of the exam will be announced by ringing a bell.
10. The final answer in each question part must be accompanied by units, which should be in SI or appropriate units. 20% of the marks available for that part will be deducted for a correct answer without units.
11. The required numerical accuracy for the final answer depends on the number of significant figures given in the data values in the problem. 20% of the marks available for the final answer in each question part will be deducted for answers without required accuracy as given in the problem. Use the constant values exactly as given in the table of constants.
12. At the end of the exam put all papers, including scratch papers, inside the envelope and leave everything on your desk.

problems.statement: Calculate the mean mass density for a super massive black hole with total mass of $1\times10^8 M_\odot$ inside the Schwarzschild radius.

solution.statement:
The Schwarzschild radius of a black hole with mass of $M$ is

$$R=\frac{2GM}{c^2}.$$

(4 points)

The mean density is

$$\rho=\frac{M}{\frac43\pi\frac{8G^3M^3}{c^6}}=\frac{3c^6}{32\pi G^3M^2}.$$

(2 points)

$$\rho=\frac{3(3\times10^8)^6}{32\pi(6.67\times10^{-11})^3(10^8\times19.99\times10^{30})^2}=1.85\times10^3\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}.$$

(4 points)

Source note: the numerical substitution prints $19.99\times10^{30}$, although the constants table gives the solar mass as $1.99\times10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg}$. The printed substitution and answer are retained.

problems.statement: Estimate the number of photons per second that arrive on our eye at $\lambda=550\ \mathrm{nm}$ (V-band) from a G2 main sequence star with apparent magnitude of $m=6$ (the threshold of naked eye visibility). Assume the eye pupil diameter is $6\ \mathrm{mm}$ and all the radition from this star is in $\lambda=550\ \mathrm{nm}$.

solution.statement:
$$m_1-m_2=-2.5\log\frac{f_1}{f_2}.$$

(1 point)

$$6-(-26.8)=-2.5\log\frac{f_1}{1.37\times10^3},\qquad f_1=1.04\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}.$$

(3 points)

The energy of each photon in V-band with wavelength of $\lambda$ is

$$E_p=h\nu=\frac{hc}{\lambda}=\frac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3\times10^8}{550\times10^{-9}}=3.62\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm J.$$

(3 points)

The number of photons which arrive to eye pupil per second is

$$N=\frac{f_1\pi r_e^2}{E_p}=\frac{1.04\times10^{-10}}{3.62\times10^{-19}}\times3.1416\times(0.003)^2=8\times10^3\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}.$$

(3 points)

problems.statement: Estimate the radius of a planet that a man can escape its gravitation by jumping vertically. Assume density of the planet and the Earth are the same.

solution.statement:
A man can jump normally about 50 cm. His initial velocity is

$$v=\sqrt{2gh}=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.5}=3.13\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.$$

(3 points)

To escape from a planet this velocity should be equal to escape velocity:

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}.$$

(3 points)

$$v^2=\frac{2GM}{R}=\frac{2G}{R}\frac{4\pi}{3}\rho R^3=\frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho R^2.$$

(2 points)

$$R^2=\frac{3v^2}{8\pi G\rho},\qquad R=2\times10^3\ \mathrm m.$$

(2 points)

problems.statement:
In a typical Persian architecture, on top of south side windows there is a structure called "Tabeshband" (shader), which controls sunlight in summer and winter. In summer when the Sun is high, Tabeshband prevents sunlight to enter rooms and keeps inside cooler. In the modern architecture it is verified that the Tabeshband saves about 20% of energy cost. Figure (1) shows a vertical section of this design at latitude of $36.0^\circ\mathrm N$ with window and Tabeshband.

Using the parameters given in the figure, calculate the maximum width of the Tabeshband, "$x$", and maximum height of the window, "$h$" in such a way that:

1. No direct sunlight can enter to the room in the summer solstice at noon.
2. The direct sunlight reaches the end of the room (indicated by the point A in the figure) in the winter solstice at noon.

![Figure (1): room with Tabeshband, H=3 m, D=4.50 m, window height h and shader width x.](#ioaa2009-tabeshband-astra-r11-20260925)

solution.statement:
Zenith angle of the Sun at noon in summer solstice is

$$z_s=\varphi-23.5^\circ=12.5^\circ.$$

(1.5 points)

Zenith angle of the Sun at noon in winter solstice is

$$z_w=\varphi+23.5^\circ=59.5^\circ.$$

(1.5 points)

In summer:

$$\tan z_s=\frac{x}{h}=0.22.$$

(1.5 points)

In winter:

$$\tan z_w=\frac{D+x}{H}=1.70.$$

(1.5 points)

$$x=1.70H-D=0.60\ \mathrm m.$$

(2 points)

$$h=2.73\ \mathrm m.$$

(2 points)

![Summer and winter sunlight geometry for the shader.](#ioaa2009-summer-winter-astra-r11-20260925)

figures.alt: Summer and winter sunlight geometry for the shader.
Figure (1): room with Tabeshband, H=3 m, D=4.50 m, window height h and shader width x.

problems.statement: The Damavand Mountain is located at the North part of Iran, in south coast of Caspian Sea. Consider an observer standing on the Damavand mountaintop (latitude = $35^\circ57'\mathrm N$; longitude = $52^\circ6'\mathrm E$; altitude $5.6\times10^3\ \mathrm m$ from the mean sea level) and looking at the sky over the Caspian Sea. What is the minimum declination for a star, to be seen marginally circumpolar for this observer. Geodetic radius of the Earth at this latitude is $6370.8\ \mathrm{km}$. Surface level of the Caspian Sea is approximately equal to the mean sea level.

solution.statement:
There are two effects to be considered: atmospheric refraction ($34'$ at the horizon; 3 points) and depression of the horizon due to the height of the observer.

$$\cos\theta=\frac{R}{R+h}=\frac{6370.8}{6370.8+5.6},\qquad\theta=2^\circ24'.$$

(3 points)

$$\delta_{\min}=90^\circ-\text{Latitude}-\text{Refraction}-\text{Horizon depression}.$$

(2 points)

$$\delta_{\min}=90^\circ-35^\circ57'-34'-2^\circ24'=51^\circ5'.$$

(2 points)

![Geometrical depression of the horizon from the mountaintop.](#ioaa2009-horizon-astra-r11-20260925)

figures.alt: Geometrical depression of the horizon from the mountaintop.

problems.statement: Derive a relation for the escape velocity of an object, launched from the center of a proto-star cloud. The cloud has uniform density with the mass of $M$ and radius $R$. Ignore collisions between the particles of the cloud and the launched object. If the object were allowed to fall freely from the surface, it would reach the center with a velocity equal to $\sqrt{GM/R}$.

solution.statement:
We calculate the potential at the center of a spherical mass with uniform density, taking the potential at infinity to be zero.

![Uniform spherical protostar cloud and the inward fall of the object.](#ioaa2009-protostar-r2-astra-r11-20260925)

$$\frac12mv^2(r=R)-\frac{GMm}{R}=E=\frac12mv^2(r=0)+\phi_0.$$

(4 points)

$$v(R)=0,\qquad v(0)=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{R}}.$$

(1 point)

$$\phi_0=-\frac12mv_0^2-\frac{GmM}{R}.$$

(1 point)

$$\phi_0=-\frac12m\left(\sqrt{\frac{GM}{R}}\right)^2-\frac{GmM}{R}=-\frac32\frac{GMm}{R}.$$

(2 points)

For escape the total energy must be zero:

$$E=\frac12mv_e^2+\phi(r=0)=\frac12mv_e^2-\frac32\frac{GMm}{R}=0.$$

$$v_e^2=\frac{3GM}{R},\qquad v_e=\sqrt{\frac{3GM}{R}}.$$

(2 points)

figures.alt: Uniform spherical protostar cloud and the inward fall of the object.

problems.statement: A student tries to measure field of view (FOV) of the eyepiece of his/her telescope, using rotation of the Earth. To do this job, the observer points the telescope towards Vega (alpha Lyr., RA: $18.5^h$, Dec: $+39^\circ$), turns off its "clock drive" and measures trace out time, $t=5.3$ minutes, that Vega crosses the full diameter of the FOV. What is the FOV of this telescope in arc-minutes?

solution.statement:
From the figure:

$$\beta=\varphi\cos\delta.$$

(4 points)

The Earth's angular velocity is

$$\omega=\frac{2\pi}{86164}=7.29\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}.$$

(2 points)

$$\varphi=\omega t=7.29\times10^{-5}\times5.3\times60=0.023\ \mathrm{rad}.$$

$$\mathrm{FOV}=\beta=0.023\cos39^\circ=0.018\ \mathrm{rad}\simeq62'.$$

(4 points)

![Celestial-sphere geometry relating angular drift to field of view.](#ioaa2009-vega-fov-astra-r11-20260925)

figures.alt: Celestial-sphere geometry relating angular drift to field of view.

problems.statement: Estimate the mass of a globular cluster with the radius of $r=20\ \mathrm{pc}$ and root mean square velocity of stars equal to $v_{\mathrm{rms}}=3\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.

solution.statement:
$$\frac12Mv_{\mathrm{esc}}^2=\frac12M\frac{2GM}{R}.$$

(4 points)

The velocity of stars must be smaller than the escape velocity. Take $v_{\mathrm{esc}}\simeq\sqrt2v_{\mathrm{rms}}$; this is an estimation and any smaller velocity is accepted. Replacing by $v_{\mathrm{rms}}$:

$$Mv_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\frac{GM^2}{R}.$$

(2 points)

$$M=\frac{Rv_{\mathrm{rms}}^2}{G}=\frac{20\times3.09\times10^{16}\times9\times10^6}{6.67\times10^{-11}}=8.3\times10^{34}\ \mathrm{kg}=4.2\times10^4M_\odot.$$

(4 points)

problems.statement: The Galactic longitude of a star is $l=15^\circ$. Its radial velocity with respect to the Sun is $V_r=100\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Assume stars in the disk of the Galaxy are orbiting the center with a constant velocity of $V_0=250\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ in circular orbits in the same sense in the galactic plane. Calculate distance of the star from the center of the Galaxy.

solution.statement:
In the figure S is the Sun, with radius $R_0$ and velocity $V_0$, and P is the star, with radius $R$ and $V=V_0$.

$$V_r=V\cos\alpha-V_0\sin l=V_0(\cos\alpha-\sin l).$$

(4 points)

From the SCP triangle:

$$\frac{\sin l}{R}=\frac{\cos\alpha}{R_0},\qquad\cos\alpha=\frac{R_0}{R}\sin l.$$

(1 point)

$$V_r=V_0\left(\frac{R_0}{R}-1\right)\sin l.$$

(2 points)

$$\frac{R_0}{R}-1=\frac{V_r}{V_0\sin l},\qquad\frac{R_0}{R}=\frac{V_r+V_0\sin l}{V_0\sin l}.$$

$$R=R_0\frac{V_0\sin l}{V_r+V_0\sin l}.$$

(2 points)

$$R=8\times10^3\frac{250\sin15^\circ}{100+250\sin15^\circ}=3\times10^3\ \mathrm{pc}.$$

(1 point)

![Galactic rotation geometry: Sun S, star P and Galactic centre C.](#ioaa2009-galactic-rotation-astra-r11-20260925)

figures.alt: Galactic rotation geometry: Sun S, star P and Galactic centre C.

problems.statement: A main sequence star with the radius and mass of $R=4R_\odot$, $M=6M_\odot$ has an average magnetic field of $1\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm T$. Calculate the strength of the magnetic field of the star when it evolves to a neutron star with the radius of $20\ \mathrm{km}$.

solution.statement:
Because of high conductivity of plasma inside the star, flux of magnetic field will be conserved through contraction then:

$$4\pi R^2B=4\pi R_n^2B_n.$$

(6 points)

Where $R_n$ and $B_n$ are radius and magnetic field of neutron star, thus:

$$B_n=\left(\frac{R}{R_n}\right)^2B=\left(\frac{4\times6.96\times10^5}{20}\right)^2.$$

(2 points)

$$B_n=1.93\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{Gauss}=1.93\times10^6\ \mathrm T.$$

(2 points)

Source note: the numerical intermediate is printed without its magnetic-field factor or a unit; the final Gauss and tesla values are retained.

problems.statement:
Assume the mass of neutrinos is $m_\nu=10^{-5}m_e$. Calculate the number density of neutrinos ($n_\nu$) needed to compensate the dark matter of the universe. Assume the universe is flat and 25% of its mass is dark matter.

Hint: Take the classical total energy equal to zero.

solution.statement:
In a flat universe

$$\rho=\rho_c=\frac{3H^2}{8\pi G}.$$

(4 points)

$$H=75\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}=2.4\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}.$$

(2 points)

$$\rho_c=1.1\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}.$$

(2 points)

$$n_\nu=\frac{0.25\rho_c}{10^{-5}m_e}=3\times10^8\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}.$$

(2 points)

problems.statement: Calculate how much the radius of the Earth's orbit increases as a result of the Sun losing mass due to the thermo-nuclear reactions in its center in 100 years. Assume the Earth's orbit remains circular during this period.

solution.statement:
The rate of change of solar mass could be estimated from solar luminosity:

$$L_\odot=-\frac{\Delta E}{\Delta t}=-\frac{\Delta Mc^2}{\Delta t}=-\dot Mc^2.$$

(2 points)

$$\dot M=-\frac{L_\odot}{c^2}=-\frac{3.83\times10^{26}}{(3.00\times10^8)^2}=-4.26\times10^9\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}.$$

Newton second law will give us:

$$\frac{v^2}{r}=\frac{GM}{r^2}\Rightarrow v^2=\frac{GM}{r}.$$

(2 points)

where $v$ and $r$ are orbital velocity and orbital radius of the Earth. From conservation of angular momentum:

$$l=rmv\Rightarrow v=\frac{l}{mr}.$$

(2 points)

Where $m$ and $l$ are the Earth mass and angular momentum which are constant:

$$\frac{l^2}{m^2r^2}=\frac{GM}{r}\Rightarrow r=\frac{l^2}{GMm^2}.$$

$$\dot r=-\frac{l^2}{Gm^2}\frac{\dot M}{M^2}=-\frac{r^2m^2v^2}{GM^2m^2}\dot M.$$

$$\dot r=-\frac{(GM/r)r^2}{G}\frac{\dot M}{M^2}=-r\frac{\dot M}{M}\Rightarrow\frac{\dot r}{r}=-\frac{\dot M}{M}\Rightarrow\dot r=-r\frac{\dot M}{M}.$$

$$\dot r=-\frac{1.50\times10^{11}\times4.26\times10^9}{1.99\times10^{30}}=3.21\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m/s}.$$

(2 points)

$$\Delta r=3.19\times10^{-10}\times100\times86400\times365.24=1.01\ \mathrm m\quad(\text{for 100 years}).$$

(2 points)

Source note: the last two lines reproduce the printed negative sign before a positive numerical numerator and the change from 3.21 to 3.19. These source inconsistencies have not been silently repaired.

problems.statement: Assume that you are living in the time of Copernicus and do not know anything about Kepler's laws. You might calculate Mars-Sun distance in the same way as he did. After accepting the revolutionary belief that all the planets are orbiting around the Sun, not around the Earth, you measure that the orbital period of Mars is 687 days, then you observe that 106 days after opposition of Mars, the planet appears in quadrature. Calculate Mars-Sun distance in astronomical unit (AU).

solution.statement:
We know the orbital period of Mars then the angle $\angle M_1SM_2$ can be determined simply

$$\angle M_1SM_2=\frac{106}{687}\times360=55.5^\circ.$$

(2 points)

By the same way we determine $\angle E_1SE_2$:

$$\angle E_1SE_2=\frac{106}{365}\times360=104.5^\circ.$$

(2 points)

Then angle $\angle M_2SE_2$ is:

$$\angle M_2SE_2=104.5-55.5=49.0^\circ.$$

(2 points)

$$\cos(\angle M_2SE_2)=\frac{SE_2}{SM_2}.$$

(2 points)

$$r_{\mathrm{mars}}=\frac{SM_2}{SE_2}=\frac1{\cos(\angle M_2SE_2)}=\frac1{\cos49.0^\circ}=1.52\ \mathrm{AU}.$$

(2 points)

![Earth and Mars at opposition and quadrature.](#ioaa2009-mars-quadrature-astra-r11-20260925)

figures.alt: Earth and Mars at opposition and quadrature.

problems.statement: A satellite is orbiting around the Earth in a circular orbit in the plane of the equator. An observer in Tehran at the latitude of $\varphi=35.6^\circ$ observes that the satellite has a zenith angle of $z=46.0^\circ$, when it transits the local meridian. Calculate the distance of the satellite from the center of the Earth (in the Earth radius unit).

solution.statement:
In the figure, the observer is at $O$ and the satellite is in $S$ the angle $\angle EOS$ will be

$$\angle EOS=180-z=180-46.0=134^\circ.$$

(2 points)

$$\delta=180-\varphi-\angle EOS=10.4^\circ.$$

(3 points)

In EOS triangle we have:

$$\frac{R_S}{\sin(\angle EOS)}=\frac R{\sin\delta}.$$

(3 points)

$$\frac{R_S}{R}=\frac{\sin(\angle EOS)}{\sin\delta}=3.98.$$

(2 points)

![Observer O, Earth centre E and satellite S.](#ioaa2009-satellite-astra-r11-20260925)

figures.alt: Observer O, Earth centre E and satellite S.

problems.statement:
An eclipsing close binary system consists of two giant stars with the same sizes. As a result of mutual gravitational force, stars are deformed from perfect sphere to the prolate spheroid with $a=2b$, where $a$ and $b$ are semi-major and semi-minor axes (the major axes are always co-linear). The inclination of the orbital plane to the plane of sky is $90^\circ$. Calculate the amplitude of light variation in magnitude ($\Delta m$) as a result of the orbital motion of two stars. Ignore temperature variation due to tidal deformation and limb darkening on the surface of the stars.

Hint: A prolate spheroid is a geometrical shape made by rotating of an ellipse around its major axis, like rugby ball or melon.

solution.statement:
Ignoring temperature variation on the stars surface, the brightness of star system will be proportional to projected surface of both stars on plane of the sky. Maximum brightness will occur when two stars are seen like figure 1 and minimum light will happen when one of the stars is in total eclipse and projected surface of the other is a circle with radius $b$ (Figure 2). In maximum brightness

$$I_{\max}\propto2\pi ab.$$

(3 points)

In minimum brightness

$$I_{\min}\propto\pi b^2.$$

(3 points)

So

$$\Delta m=-2.5\log\frac{I_{\max}}{I_{\min}}=-2.5\log\frac{2\pi ab}{\pi b^2}=-2.5\log4.$$

(2 points)

$$\Delta m=-1.5.$$

(2 points)

Source note: the solution refers to Figures 1 and 2, but neither is present in this solution's pages. The printed signed result is −1.5; no missing figures or sign correction are invented.

answer.note: Signed result as printed in official solution.

problems.title: High Altitude Projectile
problems.statement: A projectile which starts from the surface of the Earth at the sea level is launched with the initial speed of $v_0=\sqrt{GM/R}$ and with the projecting angle (with respect to the local horizon) of $\theta=\pi/6$. $M$ and $R$ are the mass and radius of the Earth respectively. Ignore the air resistance and rotation of the Earth.

parts.label: a
parts.statement: Show that the orbit of the projectile is an ellipse with a semi-major axis of $a=R$.

parts.label: b
parts.statement: Calculate the highest altitude of the projectile with respect to the Earth surface (in the unit of the Earth radius).

parts.label: c
parts.statement: What is the range of the projectile (distance between launching point and falling point) in the units of the earth radii?

parts.label: d
parts.statement: What is eccentricity (e) of this elliptical orbit?

parts.label: e
parts.statement: Find the time of flight for the projectile.

figures.alt: Figure (1): Earth and the elliptical projectile orbit.
figures.caption: Figure (1)

figures.alt: Figure (2): projectile orbit with projection angle theta.
figures.caption: Figure (2)

figures.alt: Area swept during the projectile flight.

sections.title: a)
sections.statement:
Total energy of the projectile is

$$E=\frac12mv_0^2-\frac{GMm}{R}=-\frac{GMm}{2R}<0.$$

$E<0$ means that orbit might be ellipse or circle. As $\theta>0$, the orbit is an ellipse. Total energy for an ellipse is

$$E=-\frac{GMm}{2a}.$$

Then

$$a=R.$$

(7 points)

sections.title: b)
sections.statement:
In figure (1) we have

$$OA+O'A=2a,\qquad O'A=a.$$

![Figure (1): Earth and the elliptical projectile orbit.](#ioaa2009-projectile-1-astra-r11-20260925)

In $OAO'$ triangle it is obvious that

$$OC=CO'.$$

Then $C$ must be the center of the ellipse with the initial velocity vector $v_0$ parallel to the ellipse major-axis ($LH$).

In figure (2)

$$HM=CH-CM=a-(R-R\sin\theta)=R-R+R\sin\theta=R\sin\theta=\frac R2.$$

(15 points)

![Figure (2): projectile orbit with projection angle theta.](#ioaa2009-projectile-2-astra-r11-20260925)

sections.title: c)
sections.statement:
Range of the projectile is $\widehat{AB}$

$$\widehat{AB}=2\left(\frac\pi2-\theta\right)R=(\pi-2\theta)R=\frac{2\pi}{3}R.$$

(6 points)

sections.title: d)
sections.statement:
Start with ellipse equation in polar coordinates

$$r=\frac{a(1-e^2)}{1+e\cos\varphi}.$$

For point A

$$R=\frac{R(1-e^2)}{1-e\cos(\frac\pi2+\theta)}.$$

$$e=\sin\theta=\frac12.$$

(5 points)

Source note: the second denominator is printed with a minus sign, although this conflicts with the displayed result. The source formula is retained.

sections.title: e)
sections.statement:
Using Kepler's second law

$$\frac{\Delta S}{S_0}=\frac{\Delta T}{T}.$$

$$\Delta S=S_{AOBH}=S_{\triangle AOB}+\frac{S_0}{2}=2\times\frac{bae}{2}+\frac{\pi ab}{2}=bae+\frac{\pi ab}{2}.$$

$$\frac{\Delta S}{S}=\frac{bae+\frac{\pi ab}{2}}{\pi ab}=\frac{e+\frac\pi2}{\pi}=\frac{0.5+\frac\pi2}{\pi}.$$

![Area swept during the projectile flight.](#ioaa2009-projectile-area-astra-r11-20260925)

Kepler's third law

$$T=\sqrt{\frac{4\pi^2R^3}{GM}}=84.5\ \mathrm{min}.$$

problems.title: Apparent number density of stars in the Galaxy
problems.statement: Let us model the number density of stars in the disk of Milky Way Galaxy with a simple exponential function of $n=n_0\exp(-(r-R_0)/R_d)$, where $r$ represents the distance from the center of the Galaxy, $R_0$ is the distance of the Sun from the center of the Galaxy, $R_d$ is the typical size of disk and $n_0$ is the stellar density of disk at the position of the Sun. An astronomer observes the center of the Galaxy within a small field of view. We take a particular type of Red giant stars (red clump) as the standard candles for the observation with approximately constant absolute magnitude of $M=-0.2$,

parts.label: a
parts.statement: Considering a limiting magnitude of $m=18$ for a telescope, calculate the maximum distance that telescope can detect the red clump stars. For simplicity we ignore the presence of interstellar medium so there is no extinction.

parts.label: b
parts.statement: Assume an extinction of $0.7\ \mathrm{mag/kpc}$ for the interstellar medium. Repeat the calculation as done in the part (a) and obtain a rough number for the maximum distance these red giant stars can be observed.

parts.label: c
parts.statement: Give an expression for the number of these red giant stars per magnitude within a solid angle of $\Omega$ that we can observe with apparent magnitude in the range of $m$ and $m+\Delta m$, (i.e. $\Delta N/\Delta m$). Red giant stars contribute fraction $f$ of overall stars. In this part assume no extinction in the interstellar medium as part (a). Assume the size of the disk is larger than maximum observable distance.

sections.title: a)
sections.statement:
Relation between the apparent and absolute magnitude is given by

$$m=M+5\log\left(\frac d{10}\right).$$

(3 points)

where $d$ is in terms of parsec. Substituting $m=18$ and $M=-0.2$, results in

$$d=4.37\times10^4\ \mathrm{pc}.$$

(5 points)

sections.title: b)
sections.statement:
Adding the term for the extinction, changes the magnitude distance relation as follows

$$m=M+0.7x+5\log(100x)$$

where $x$ is given in terms of kilo parsec. To have a rough value for $x$, after substituting $m$ and $M$, this equation reduces to

$$8.2=0.7x+5\log x.$$

(6 points)

To solve this equation we examine

$$x=5,5.5,6,6.5$$

where the best value is obtained roughly $x\simeq6.1\ \mathrm{kpc}$.

(8 points)

sections.title: c)
sections.statement:
For a solid angle $\Omega$, the number of observed red clump stars at the distance in the range of $x$ and $x+\Delta x$ is given by

$$\Delta N=\Omega x^2n(x)f\Delta x.$$

So the number of stars observed in $\Delta x$ is given by

$$\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta x}=\Omega x^2n(x)f.$$

(6 points)

From the relation between the distance and apparent magnitude we have

$$m_1=M+5\log\left(\frac x{10}\right),\qquad m_2=M+5\log\left(\frac{x+\Delta x}{10}\right).$$

$$\Delta m=5\log\left(\frac{x+\Delta x}{x}\right)=5\log\left(1+\frac{\Delta x}{x}\right).$$

$$\Delta m=\frac5{\ln10}\ln\left(1+\frac{\Delta x}{x}\right)=\frac5{\ln10}\left(\frac{\Delta x}{x}\right).$$

Replacing $\Delta x$ with $\Delta m$, results in

$$\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta m}=\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta x}\times\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta m}.$$

So the number of stars for a given magnitude is obtained by

$$\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta m}=\frac{\Omega\ln10}{5}n(x)x^3f.$$

(5 points)

Finally we substituting $x$ in terms of apparent magnitude using $x=10^{(m+5.2)/5}$. In the case of no extinction, we are able to observe the Galaxy beyond the center. So $dN/dm$ has two terms in $x<R_0$ and $x>R_0$. The relation between $x$ and $r$ for these two cases are

$$x=R_0-r\quad x<R_0$$

and

$$x=R_0+r\quad x>R_0.$$

(6 points)

$$\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta m}=\frac{\Omega\ln10}{5}n_0\exp\left(\frac{10^{(m-5.2)/5}}{R_d}\right)10^{3(m-5.2)/5}f,\qquad x<R_0.$$

$$\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta m}=\frac{\Omega\ln10}{5}n_0\exp\left(\frac{2R_0}{R_d}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{10^{(m-5.2)/5}}{R_d}\right)10^{3(m-5.2)/5}f\Theta(x_0-x),\qquad x>R_0.$$

(6 points)

where $\Theta(x)$ is the step function and $x_0$ is the maximum observable distance.

Source note: the final formulas print $m-5.2$, whereas the preceding substitution prints $m+5.2$. Both are retained as printed.
